content: The use of 4% vaginal cream has been associated with a higher incidence of headaches, reported in 26% of patients compared to 1% and 0% in the vehicle placebo and placebo groups, respectively. Other adverse effects reported with the 4% vaginal cream include dysmenorrhea, which occurred in 6% of patients compared to 2% with placebo, and fever, reported in 1% of patients compared to 3% with placebo. In clinical trials evaluating an 8% vaginal cream regimen for three days, headaches were reported in 21% of patients compared to 16% with placebo. Dysmenorrhea was also observed in 6% of patients using the 8% vaginal cream compared to 2% with placebo. Additionally, adverse events such as fever were reported in 4% of patients using the 8% vaginal cream compared to 1% with placebo. During controlled clinical studies conducted in the United States, 284 patients with vulvovaginal candidiasis were treated with TERAZOL® 3 (terconazole) 80 mg vaginal suppositories. Adverse events reported included headaches in 3% of patients compared to 2% and 7% in the vehicle placebo and placebo groups, respectively. Other adverse effects included vulvovaginal burning, reported in 2% of patients compared to 9% and 7% with placebo, and abdominal pain, observed in 8% of patients compared to 8% and 7% with placebo. Post-marketing experience with TERAZOL® has identified additional adverse drug reactions. However, because these reactions are reported voluntarily from a population of uncertain size, it is not always possible to reliably estimate their frequency or establish a causal relationship to drug exposure.
